title: Korean Galbi (Grilled Short Ribs)
summary: Flanken-cut short ribs in a sweet-savory soy and Asian pear marinade, grilled hot and fast Korean BBQ-style.
story: Galbi is Korea's backyard barbecue: thin-cut short ribs soaked overnight in soy, sugar, garlic, and grated Asian pear — the pear tenderizes and sweetens at once. Then screaming-hot grill, a few minutes a side, wrapped in lettuce with ssamjang and kimchi. Fast, loud, and gone in minutes.

items: 4 lbs beef short ribs, flanken cut 1/2-inch thick

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk the marinade, pour over the ribs, and refrigerate overnight — 8 hours minimum.

steps.title: Grill hot
steps.body: Grill over screaming-hot charcoal 3-4 minutes per side until caramelized at the edges.

steps.title: Wrap and eat
steps.body: Serve with lettuce, ssamjang, kimchi, and rice. Wrap a bite of everything and eat it in one go — that's the way.

title: Filipino Pork BBQ Skewers
summary: The Philippines' street-corner classic: pork in a sweet banana-ketchup marinade, skewered and grilled over hot coals.
story: Walk past any grill in the Philippines and you'll smell these — pork shoulder soaked overnight in banana ketchup, soy, calamansi, and brown sugar, then grilled fast over screaming coals until the edges char and caramelize. Sweet, sticky, smoky. Make extra; they disappear.

items: 3 lbs pork shoulder, sliced thin (about 1/4 inch)

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk the marinade and pour over the pork. Refrigerate overnight — 8 hours minimum for the full sweet-savory soak.

steps.title: Skewer
steps.body: Thread the pork onto bamboo skewers (soaked 30 minutes so they don't burn), weaving the slices accordion-style.

steps.title: Grill hot
steps.body: Grill over hot charcoal 3-4 minutes per side, basting with the reserved marinade, until charred at the edges and cooked through.

title: Yakitori (Chicken & Negi Skewers)
summary: Japan's charcoal-grilled chicken skewers — thigh and negi onion, brushed with sweet-savory tare over blazing coals.
story: Yakitori is Japanese barbecue stripped to the essentials: chicken thigh, long green onion, blazing binchotan charcoal, and tare — a syrupy glaze of soy, mirin, sake, and sugar. The trick is brushing the tare on again and again until the skewers shine like lacquer. Salt-and-pepper (shio) is the purist's move; tare is the crowd-pleaser.

items: 2 lbs boneless skin-on chicken thighs, cut in 1-inch cubes
4 stalks negi (long green onion), cut in 1 1/2-inch pieces

steps.title: Make the tare
steps.body: Simmer the tare ingredients 10 minutes until slightly syrupy. Set aside — this is liquid gold.

steps.title: Skewer
steps.body: Alternate chicken and negi on the skewers, packing them snug.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over the hottest charcoal you've got, turning often and brushing with tare every turn, 8-10 minutes until the chicken hits 165°F and shines.

title: Russian Shashlik
summary: Russia's iconic pork-neck kebab: onion and vinegar marinade, skewered tight, grilled over gray coals.
story: Shashlik is Russia's answer to barbecue — pork neck (the fattiest, juiciest cut) drowned in sliced onion, vinegar, salt, and pepper, then grilled over coals burned down to gray ash. The Soviet-era classic uses nothing fancier than that, and it's perfect. Serve it with pickled onions and don't you dare use a fork.

items: 4 lbs pork neck, cut in 2-inch cubes
3 large onions, sliced in thick rings

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Squeeze half the onion rings with your hands to release the juice, then mix everything with the pork. Dissolve the vinegar in the water and pour over. Refrigerate 6 hours to overnight — longer is better.

steps.title: Skewer
steps.body: Thread the pork tightly onto flat metal skewers, alternating with onion rings. Tight packing keeps the meat juicy.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over coals burned to gray-white ash — no open flame. Turn frequently, 15-20 minutes, sprinkling with water if flames flare. Cut one open to check; serve on the skewer with pickled onions.

title: German Schwenkbraten
summary: Saarland's swinging-grate pork steaks — mustard, onion, and juniper marinade over beechwood fire.
story: Yes, the Germans barbecue — and in Saarland they take it seriously. Thick pork neck steaks marinate a full day in mustard, onion, juniper, and paprika, then grill on a swinging grate (the Schwenker) over beechwood embers. Serve it with potato salad, a crusty roll, and a cold beer, the way it's done.

items: 4 pork neck steaks, about 8 oz each, 1 1/2 inches thick

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Rub the pork with the mustard, then mix with all marinade ingredients. Refrigerate 24-48 hours — the long soak is what makes it Schwenkbraten.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Shake off the excess marinade. Grill over medium beechwood or charcoal embers about 10 minutes per side to 145°F internal, grilling the onion slices alongside.

steps.title: Rest
steps.body: Rest 5 minutes. Serve with potato salad, crusty rolls, and beer.

title: Chicken Satay with Peanut Sauce
summary: Thai-style turmeric chicken skewers over hot coals, with a rich coconut-peanut dipping sauce.
story: Satay is Southeast Asia's great street food — chicken strips in a turmeric-coconut marinade, grilled fast over charcoal, dunked in peanut sauce. The marinade does double duty: color, flavor, and just enough sugar to char at the edges. Don't skimp on the peanut sauce; it's half the dish.

items: 2 lbs chicken thigh, cut in long strips

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Coat the chicken in the marinade and refrigerate at least 2 hours, up to overnight. Thread onto skewers.

steps.title: Make the sauce
steps.body: Simmer the peanut sauce ingredients 5 minutes, whisking, until smooth and glossy. Thin with a splash of water if needed.

steps.title: Grill
steps.body: Grill over hot charcoal 3-4 minutes per side until lightly charred and 165°F inside. Serve with the warm peanut sauce, cucumber, and red onion.

title: Tacos al Pastor
summary: Achiote-marinated pork stacked trompo-style with pineapple on top — the taco that Lebanese immigrants gave Mexico.
story: Al pastor is shawarma's Mexican grandchild: Lebanese immigrants brought the vertical spit, Mexico gave it achiote, dried chiles, and pineapple. At home, stack the marinated pork on a vertical skewer (or just grill it hot in batches) with a pineapple on top, shave it thin, and build tacos with charred pineapple, onion, and cilantro.

items: 4 dried guajillo chiles, stemmed, seeded, and soaked

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Blend the adobo ingredients smooth and coat the pork. Refrigerate overnight — the achiote needs time to work.

steps.title: Stack
steps.body: Stack the pork on a vertical skewer set in a halved onion base, crowned with the pineapple (trompo-style). No vertical setup? Just grill the slices hot in batches.

steps.title: Cook
steps.body: Roast or grill, turning, until the edges crisp and char — about 45-60 minutes on a trompo, less in batches. Shave thin.

steps.title: Build tacos
steps.body: Pile onto warm corn tortillas with charred pineapple chunks, onion, cilantro, and lime.

title: Hawaiian Huli Huli Chicken
summary: Hawaii's roadside legend: chicken in a soy-pineapple-ginger glaze, turned again and again over the fire.
story: Huli huli means 'turn turn' — and that's the whole technique. Since 1955, when Ernest Morgado grilled it for a farmers' gathering, this soy-pineapple-ginger chicken has been Hawaii's fundraiser and roadside staple. Marinate it, grill it, and keep turning and basting until the glaze caramelizes dark and sticky. Grill some pineapple rings alongside — that's not optional.

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Whisk the marinade ingredients. Reserve 1 cup for basting; pour the rest over the chicken and refrigerate 4 hours or overnight.

steps.title: Grill and turn
steps.body: Grill over medium heat, turning every 5 minutes and basting with the reserved marinade — huli huli, turn turn — about 35-45 minutes.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Cook to 165°F internal with a dark caramelized glaze. Rest 10 minutes. Serve with grilled pineapple and rice.

title: Israeli Shishlik
summary: Israel's backyard skewers: cumin-and-paprika chicken grilled over coals, served with hummus and Israeli salad.
story: In Israel, barbecue is 'al ha'esh' — on the fire — and shishlik is the weeknight hero: chicken cubes in olive oil, lemon, cumin, and paprika, grilled fast over hot coals. No fancy equipment, no long smoke, just bold spice and fire. Pile it into pita with hummus, Israeli salad, and a squeeze of lemon, and dinner's done.

items: 2 1/2 lbs boneless chicken thighs, cut in 1 1/2-inch cubes
Israeli salad (diced tomato, cucumber, red onion, parsley, lemon)

steps.title: Marinate
steps.body: Toss the chicken cubes in all the marinade ingredients. Refrigerate at least 1 hour, up to 8.

steps.title: Skewer and grill
steps.body: Thread onto skewers. Grill hot, 3-4 minutes per side, until charred at the edges and 165°F internal.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Slide into warm pita with hummus, Israeli salad, and lemon. Eat over the plate — it drips.

title: South African Boerewors
summary: The coil sausage of the South African braai: coriander-scented beef and pork, grilled in one long spiral.
story: Boerewors — 'farmer's sausage' — is the heart of the South African braai. By law it's mostly meat, but the soul is in the spice: toasted coriander above all, with nutmeg, cloves, and black pepper behind it. It's made and grilled in one long coil, never links. If you've got a grinder and stuffer, make it from scratch; if not, find a South African butcher and grill it right — medium coals, turned gently, never pierced.

steps.title: Grind
steps.body: Chill the meat and fat until nearly frozen. Grind through a coarse plate into a cold bowl.

steps.title: Season and mix
steps.body: Add the vinegar and spices. Mix with cold hands just until tacky — don't overwork it. Fry a small patty and adjust salt.

steps.title: Stuff
steps.body: Stuff into hog casings in one continuous coil — no links. Prick any air pockets.

steps.title: Braai
steps.body: Grill over medium coals 20-25 minutes, turning gently, to 160°F internal. Never pierce the casing. Slice the coil at the table.

title: Ember Southwest Rub
summary: Chipotle, cumin, and Hatch chile — the dry half of the Ember Southwest lineup.
story: Every sauce needs its rub. This is the dry half of the Southwest lineup: chipotle for smoke, cumin for earth, Hatch chile powder for that New Mexico kick Kelly loves, and brown sugar to caramelize it all. Rub it on the Hatch thighs, dust it over wings, or shake it on ribs — then finish with the Ember Southwest BBQ Sauce.

items: 1 Tbsp Hatch green chile powder (or New Mexico chile powder)

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Whisk everything together, breaking up any lumps in the brown sugar.

steps.title: Store
steps.body: Keep in an airtight jar away from heat and light. Good for 6 months.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: Rub generously on chicken, pork, or beef 1 hour before cooking (overnight for big cuts). Pair with Ember Southwest BBQ Sauce.

title: Smoked Barbecue Chicken
summary: A whole bird spatchcocked and halved, rubbed with Ember rub and finished with a sticky Ember sauce glaze. The backyard bird done right.
story: Halves are the working man's chicken — cheaper than breasts, more forgiving than a whole bird, and every piece gets smoke and sauce. Take a whole chicken, spatchcock it, and cut it in half. Season with Ember rub, smoke it steady, and don't sauce too early or the sugar burns before the meat's done. This is Kelly's backyard bird, the one from the grill photo.

items: Ember rub (or your favorite rub), enough to coat
1 cup Ember sauce (or your favorite barbecue sauce), thinned with a splash of apple juice if it's thick

steps.title: Spatchcock and halve
steps.body: Cut out the backbone, press the breast flat, then cut the bird in half through the breastbone. Pat dry. Season all over with Ember rub — under the skin where you can reach.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 275–300°F with hickory or apple, skin-side up. About 2 to 2½ hours.

steps.title: Glaze — your call
steps.body: When the thighs read 165°F, it’s your choice: brush on the Ember sauce and give it 20–30 more minutes so the glaze sets and gets sticky, or leave the bird dry if you like the bark just the way it is.

steps.title: Rest and serve
steps.body: Pull at 175°F in the thigh (breast 160°F). Rest 10 minutes, then cut each half into leg and breast portions.

proTips.text: Sauce late — if you sauce at all. Sugar burns, so the glaze goes on in the last half hour, not the first. No sauce? The bark stands on its own.
Halves over direct heat for the last 5 minutes if you want the skin to bite through.

title: Smoked Canadian Bacon
summary: Turn a pork loin into deli-style Canadian bacon with a simple 7-day cure and a kiss of smoke.
story: Canadian bacon isn't bacon at all — it's cured pork loin, smoked gentle and sliced thin. The cure does the real work over a week in the fridge; the smoker just finishes the job. Slice it thin for breakfast sandwiches, chop it into hash, or eat it cold right off the slicer.

items: 1 whole pork loin, 3–4 lbs, trimmed of excess fat and silverskin

steps.title: Mix the cure
steps.body: Stir the kosher salt, brown sugar, pink curing salt, black pepper, garlic powder, and onion powder together in a bowl.

steps.title: Rub the loin
steps.body: Coat the pork loin all over with the cure — every surface, no bare spots.

steps.title: Cure 7 days
steps.body: Seal the loin in a large zip-top or vacuum bag, squeezing out the air. Set it on a tray in the fridge and flip the bag once a day for 7 days. It will release liquid — that's normal.

steps.title: Rinse and dry
steps.body: Rinse the loin under cold water and pat dry. Set it on a rack over a tray, uncovered, in the fridge overnight. The dry surface takes smoke better.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Run the smoker at 200–225°F with fruit wood or hickory. Smoke the loin to 145°F internal, about 2 to 3 hours.

steps.title: Rest, chill, slice
steps.body: Rest 20 minutes, then chill fully in the fridge before slicing thin, like deli meat.

proTips.text: Don't skip the pink curing salt — it's what keeps the meat rosy and safe through the long cure. 1 teaspoon per 5 lbs of meat is the rule.
Chill it firm before slicing — a cold loin cuts thin and even. Fry slices for breakfast sandwiches or chop into hash.

title: Kelly's Smoked Baby Back Ribs
summary: Real ribs off Kelly's smoker — sweet heat, crackly crust, clean bite off the bone.
story: Baby backs are the leaner, quicker rib — they take smoke beautifully and don't need all day. The crust is the thing: a little turbinado sugar over the rub goes crackly under the heat, and the sauce goes on late so it sets instead of burns.

items: Ember rub (or your favorite rib rub), enough to coat
Ember sauce (or your favorite barbecue sauce), for glazing
Butter, brown sugar, honey, and a sprinkle of rub (for wrapping, optional)

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Pull the membrane from the bone side. Coat the racks all over with Ember rub, then a light shake of turbinado sugar over the top.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 250°F with hickory or oak, bone-side down, about 3 hours — until the bark sets and the color goes deep.

steps.title: Wrap or ride it out
steps.body: Your choice: wrap in foil with pats of butter, a handful of brown sugar, a drizzle of honey, a sprinkle of extra rub, and a splash of cherry Dr Pepper or whatever flavor soda you like for about an hour for bend-tender ribs, or skip the wrap and ride it out for a firmer bite.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Brush on the Ember sauce and give it 20–30 minutes so the glaze sets sticky.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes, then slice between the bones.

proTips.text: Turbinado for the crust — crackly, not burnt.
Sauce late. Sugar burns — the glaze goes on at the end.
Cherry Dr Pepper mixed with brown sugar, mopped or sprayed on during the cook, builds a crackling bark.

title: Smoked Pork Tenderloin
summary: Smoke it gentle, then char it like a steakhouse steak — juicy, barely pink, crosshatch crust.
story: There's a hundred ways to do a tenderloin, but treat it like a good steak and it eats like one. Smoke brings the flavor; a screaming-hot finish on GrillGrates brings the crust. Pull it at 155°F and it stays juicy with just a blush of pink.

items: 1–2 pork tenderloins, about 1 lb each, silverskin trimmed
Ember rub (or your favorite steak seasoning), enough to coat
Light coat of olive oil or yellow mustard as a binder

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Trim the silverskin. Rub with a light coat of oil or mustard, then season all over with Ember rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 250°F with apple or cherry wood. Smoke to about 140°F internal — roughly an hour.

steps.title: Char it
steps.body: Move to screaming-hot GrillGrates over direct heat. Roll the tenderloins to char all sides with crosshatch marks, pulling at 155°F internal.

steps.title: Rest and slice
steps.body: Rest 10 minutes, then slice into medallions. Barely pink, juicy, steakhouse crust.

proTips.text: I run mine to 155°F — stays juicy with just a blush of pink. Don't let it ride past that.
GrillGrates are worth it — that crosshatch char eats like a professional steakhouse.

title: Smoked Pork Chops
summary: Thick-cut chops with a kiss of smoke, finished like a steak — crosshatch char and a sticky Ember glaze.
story: A thick pork chop wants the same treatment as a good steak. Start it low so it takes on a little smoke, then move it over direct heat on the GrillGrates and char it with crosshatch marks. Brush on the Ember Finishing Glaze at the end, pull it at 155°F, and it stays juicy. No wrapping — a chop this thick doesn't need it.

items: Mayonnaise or yellow mustard, a thin coat as a binder
Ember rub (or your favorite pork rub), enough to coat
½ cup Ember Finishing Glaze (or your favorite barbecue sauce)

steps.title: Prep
steps.body: Pat the chops dry. Smear on a thin coat of mayonnaise or mustard as a binder, then season all over with Ember rub.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 250°F with apple or cherry wood. Smoke the chops to about 135°F internal — roughly 45 minutes to an hour, depending on thickness.

steps.title: Char and glaze
steps.body: Move the chops to screaming-hot GrillGrates over direct heat. Sear with crosshatch marks, turning once, and brush on the Ember Finishing Glaze in the last minute or two. Pull at 155°F internal.

steps.title: Rest and serve
steps.body: Rest 5–10 minutes so the juices settle, then serve. Juicy and smoky, with a steakhouse char.

proTips.text: I never wrap my pork chops. A thick chop doesn't need it — the smoke and the char do all the work.
Treat the finish like a steak: hot grates, crosshatch marks, and don't let it ride past 155°F or it'll dry out.

title: Smoked Barbecue Meatballs
summary: Beef-and-pork meatballs smoked low, then glazed with Ember sauce and cherry preserves — sweet, a little tart, sticky.
story: Everybody knows the grape-jelly potluck meatball. This is the pit version: real smoke first, then a cherry glaze. Cherry belongs with beef and pork — it's the same fruit behind the cherry Dr Pepper bark trick — and it makes these yours instead of a copy of everybody else's.

items: 2 Tbsp Ember rub (or your favorite rub), plus a little extra for dusting
1 cup Ember sauce (or your favorite barbecue sauce)
½ tsp red pepper flakes (optional, for heat)

steps.title: Mix
steps.body: Mix everything gentle, just until it comes together. Overworking the mix is what makes meatballs eat like hockey pucks.

steps.title: Roll and chill
steps.body: Roll into balls about 1½ inches across — wet hands keep the mix from sticking to you. You should get about 24. Rest them in the fridge 20–30 minutes so they hold their shape on the pit.

steps.title: Smoke
steps.body: Pit at 250°F with apple or cherry wood. Dust the tops with a little more rub and smoke about an hour, until they hit 160°F inside.

steps.title: Glaze
steps.body: Warm the Ember sauce and cherry preserves together until the preserves melt in — stir in the red pepper flakes if you're using them. Brush the glaze over the meatballs and give them 10–15 more minutes so it sets sticky.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: Serve them as a pick-up appetizer with toothpicks, or pile them up as a main.

proTips.text: You can put red pepper flakes in it if you want to make them spicier.
Don't overmix — gentle hands keep them tender.
